rationale: These recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blink, movement or electrode-pop windows can inflate the mean Welch spectrum, mostly in delta and theta. This change takes the median across the 2-s windows instead of the mean. The median gives a spectrum that ignores those transient artifacts, so band powers should reflect background resting activity better and hold up across clinics.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so the mean-averaged Welch PSD can be dominated by a few windows with blinks, movement or electrode pops. Those mostly inflate delta and broadband power and distort relative band power. This change switches to median-averaged Welch (`average="median"`), which ignores those outlier windows. It should give cleaner, more reproducible subject spectra here and on the external clinic data. Everything else stays the same. I haven't run it, so I don't know its Dev score yet.

I'm adding one aperiodic (1/f) slope per channel and condition. It's fitted to the log-log Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. MDD has been linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up in the aperiodic exponent, and relative band power mixes that slope with the oscillatory peaks. The slope also doesn't change with amplitude scale, which helps on the external Mumtaz set. I leave the offset out because it depends on amplitude scale.

These recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blink, movement or electrode-pop segments can inflate the mean-averaged Welch PSD, mostly in the delta and gamma bands, and that distorts the relative band powers. Switching to median-averaged Welch over 2 s segments rejects those transient artifacts. This should make the spectral biomarker cleaner and more robust across clinics, while the features and classifier stay the same.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so the mean-averaged Welch PSD gets pulled around by a few windows with blinks, movement or electrode pops, and that noise lands in the band powers. Averaging the per-window spectra with the median (`average="median"`) should give cleaner, artifact-robust spectra for both the dev data and the external clinic set. Everything else stays the same; the scaling bias of the median estimate cancels out in relative power.

The recordings are raw, with no artifact rejection, so eye blinks, movement and electrode pops in a few 2-s segments can dominate Welch's mean-averaged PSD. Under this hypothesis, those artifacts add noise to the relative band powers in the delta and gamma bands especially. Switching to median averaging across Welch segments should reject these outliers without changing the feature set or the model. It should also travel better to the external clinic's data.

I'm adding one 1/f exponent per channel and condition, alongside the existing relative band powers. It's the slope of a straight-line fit to the log-log Welch spectrum over 2–7 Hz and 14–40 Hz, which leaves out the alpha peak and line noise. This exponent is altered in depression (thought to reflect excitation/inhibition balance), the current features don't capture it, and a slope ignores amplitude scale, which should help on the external dataset.

I'm adding a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each condition. It comes from a log-log line fit of the Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, with the 7–14 Hz alpha range left out so the alpha peak doesn't bias the slope. The exponent tracks the brain's excitation/inhibition balance, which has been reported as altered in depression. Relative band power can't fully capture it because the 1/f shape and band peaks get mixed together. It also doesn't change with amplitude scale (the fit's intercept would, so I leave it out), which matters for the external Mumtaz set. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats the current Dev score of 0.857.

These recordings have had no artifact rejection, so eye blinks, movement and electrode pops can dominate a mean-averaged Welch PSD, mostly in the delta and theta bands and in the eyes-open condition. Switching Welch to median averaging across segments should give artifact-robust band-power estimates without dropping any data, and nothing else changes.

I'm adding one 1/f (aperiodic) spectral slope per channel and condition. It's a log-log line fitted over 2–7 Hz and 14–40 Hz, skipping the alpha peak. Depression has been linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, and the slope tracks that. Relative band power can't fully capture it. The slope also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, so it should hold up on the external dataset.

The recordings have had no artifact rejection, so a few eye blinks, movement or muscle bursts can dominate the mean Welch spectrum. That inflates delta and gamma and distorts the relative band powers. Averaging the per-segment periodograms with the median (`average='median'`) is a robust estimate of the spectrum that ignores sparse artifact segments. It should give cleaner per-subject band profiles that are less specific to the recording site, for both the dev score and the external Mumtaz set.

I'm splitting alpha into 8–10 and 10–13 Hz and beta into 13–20 and 20–30 Hz. In depression, low alpha, high alpha and low/high beta are reported to change in different directions, and averaging them inside one broad band can cancel those effects out. Everything else stays the same, so any change in score comes only from the finer bands, and the features remain scale-invariant relative powers.

I'm adding a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each condition. It comes from a log-log linear fit of the Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, with the 7–14 Hz alpha range left out so the alpha peak doesn't bias the slope. Changes in the 1/f slope (often read as a marker of the excitation/inhibition balance) have been reported in depression, and relative band power doesn't capture them separately from oscillatory peaks. The slope is also unaffected by amplitude scaling, which matters for the external dataset. I haven't run this change, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

I'm adding a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each condition to the existing relative band powers. The exponent is fitted on the log-log Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. Depression has been linked to changes in the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain, and the 1/f exponent is one way to measure that. I keep only the slope and drop the offset, so the new features don't depend on amplitude scale and should still hold on recordings from other amplifiers.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so the mean-averaged Welch PSD gets inflated by occasional blinks, movement and muscle bursts, which mostly hit delta and gamma and add noise across subjects. I'm switching to median averaging across Welch segments. This rejects artifacts per segment and per frequency bin without changing any of the features, and it should also hold up better on the external Mumtaz recordings.

I'm splitting the coarse alpha and beta bands into sub-bands: alpha1 8–10 Hz, alpha2 10–13 Hz, beta1 13–20 Hz and beta2 20–30 Hz. MDD findings are band-specific (for example, low-alpha excess and changes in fast beta), and the wide 8–13 and 13–30 Hz bins can average these effects away. The features stay as log relative power, so they remain robust to amplitude scale on the external set.

I'm adding a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) slope for each condition alongside the existing log relative band powers. The slope is fitted to the log-log Welch spectrum over 2–40 Hz, skipping the alpha range (7–14 Hz). The 1/f slope is thought to track the cortical balance of excitation and inhibition, which is reported to change in depression. Band-power ratios mix that slope with true oscillatory power, so the slope adds complementary information. It also doesn't depend on amplitude scale, which should help when the model is applied to the external Mumtaz data. I haven't run this yet, so I don't know whether it beats the current 0.857.

I'm re-referencing every recording to the common average before computing the Welch PSD, with no other changes. The data keep their original reference, so the power on each channel depends on the reference electrode. The external Mumtaz set uses a different amplifier and reference. Averaging the reference removes that shared signal, which should make the per-channel relative band powers more comparable between subjects and clinics, and probably sharpens the spatial pattern in theta and alpha.

I'm adding a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent next to the existing relative band powers. It is the slope of log-power against log-frequency over 2–40 Hz, with the 7–14 Hz alpha peak left out. MDD has been linked to a shifted excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up as a change in this broadband slope, and relative band powers only capture it indirectly. The exponent also ignores overall amplitude, so it should hold up on the external amplifier.

I'm splitting alpha into low and high (8–10 and 10–13 Hz) and beta into low and high (13–20 and 20–30 Hz). In MDD the spectral effects tend to be specific to these sub-bands, such as raised low-alpha power and changes in fast beta, and the broad 8–13 and 13–30 Hz bands blur them together. The features stay log relative power, which keeps them robust to amplitude scale. Everything else is unchanged; I haven't run it, so I don't know the new score yet.
